hints: Think about what ideal means for an amplifier - it should amplify perfectly without loading the circuit before it and without losing voltage in itself.
Focus on one input idea and one output idea - what should the resistance looking into the inputs be, and what should the resistance looking out of the output be for perfect behaviour?
walkthrough:
**What ideal really means**
An ideal op-amp is a perfect voltage amplifier. You can remember it as having perfect input behaviour and perfect output behaviour. At the input it should take a voltage signal without drawing any current, and it should turn even the tiniest input difference into a huge output.

**Pick two clean properties**
Good pairs to state are: infinite open-loop gain, so $$V_{out} = A_0(V_+ - V_-)$$ is enormous, and infinite input impedance, so no current flows into the $+$ and $-$ inputs. Alternatives that also earn credit are zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth and infinite slew rate.
Final answer: Any two from: infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, infinite bandwidth, infinite slew rate.

hints: Look at the left potential divider - one resistor is variable V, the other X has the sloping line for a sensor. Which sensor changes resistance with temperature and is used with an op-amp for temperature sensing?
walkthrough:
**Reading the symbols**
On the left, X is drawn in series with variable resistor V between $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$. Its symbol with the diagonal arrow and temperature link is the thermistor, whose resistance changes with temperature. On the right, the dashed box Y contains a coil that controls a switch in the lamp circuit. That is the classic relay symbol.

**Why they fit here**
The thermistor senses temperature and changes $V_-$ at the inverting input. The coil Y is energised by the op-amp output current through the diode, closing the switch and letting the lamp L light. So X: thermistor, Y: relay.
Final answer: X is a thermistor (NTC thermistor) and Y is a relay (electromagnetic relay coil with switch).

hints: Check for a feedback connection from output back to input in Fig. 7.1 - is there any resistor linking output to the $-$ input to control the gain?
Recall how huge the open-loop gain $A_0$ is, so think what even a tiny $V_+ - V_-$ will do to $A_0(V_+ - V_-)$ compared with the $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$ supplies.
walkthrough:
**No feedback means full gain**
In Fig. 7.1 the output goes only to the diode and relay, there is no connection back to the $-$ input. That means the gain is the full open-loop gain $A_0$, which for an ideal op-amp is infinite and for a real op-amp is still typically $10^5$.

**Why only saturation is possible**
With $$V_{out} = A_0(V_+ - V_-)$$ even a fraction of a millivolt difference would try to give hundreds of volts. The output cannot exceed the supply rails, about $+5\text{ V}$ to $-5\text{ V}$ here, so it saturates. If $V_+ > V_-$ it saturates positively, if $V_- > V_+$ it saturates negatively. Those are the only two stable states.

Final answer: There is no (negative) feedback so the op-amp is open-loop with very high gain. Any difference between $V_+$ and $V_-$ drives the output to saturation, positively if $V_+ > V_-$ and negatively if $V_- > V_+$.

hints: Think of the special name for an open-loop op-amp that simply compares the two input voltages and switches high or low to tell you which is larger.
walkthrough:
**Comparing two voltages**
This circuit does not amplify a small signal smoothly, it just decides which input is bigger. When $V_+$ is higher the output goes high, when $V_-$ is higher the output goes low. A circuit used in exactly this switching way is called a comparator.

hints: Start with the fixed $V_+$ divider - two identical resistors R between $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$. What is $V_+$? Then think how $V_-$ from the V-X divider moves when X gets hot.
Link the output polarity to the lamp - a positive output can pass the diode and energise the relay coil to close the switch, a negative output cannot. So which temperature makes $V_+ > V_-$?
walkthrough:
**Find the reference voltage**
The $+$ input is held by two equal resistors R between $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$, so $$V_+ = 0\text{ V}$$ at the midpoint. The $-$ input is the midpoint of V on top and thermistor X below.

**How temperature switches the output**
For an NTC thermistor, resistance falls as temperature rises. When it is hot, resistance of X is small, so most of the $10\text{ V}$ drop is across V and $V_-$ is pulled down below $0\text{ V}$. Then $V_+ > V_-$ and the output saturates positively. That forward biases the diode, current flows through relay coil Y to $-5\text{ V}$, the relay closes and lamp L connects between $+5\text{ V}$ and $-5\text{ V}$ and lights. When cold, $V_- > V_+$, output is negative, diode blocks, relay is off and lamp is off. So the lamp lights when temperature is above the set threshold.

Final answer: Lamp L lights when temperature is above a particular (threshold) value. At high temperature the thermistor resistance falls so $V_-$ falls below $V_+$, output saturates positively, diode conducts, relay is energised and switch closes.

hints: Since V sets the value of $V_-$ that must be beaten by the thermistor divider, think what changing V lets you choose about when the switching happens.
walkthrough:
**Setting the trip point**
Changing variable resistor V changes the potential divider ratio on the $-$ side and so changes the value of thermistor resistance, and hence temperature, needed to make $V_-$ cross $V_+$. In other words V lets you pre-set or calibrate the threshold temperature at which the comparator switches and the lamp lights.
Final answer: To adjust (vary) the temperature at which the lamp switches on/off, by changing the threshold voltage at the inverting input.
